title: Permutations and Combinations
description: Comprehensive shared preparation notes and worked practice for Permutations and Combinations. Review the target examination syllabus and level before reuse.

coverage: Combinations when order does not matter

sections.label: Concepts and worked examples
sections.html:
Counting principle and factorials

If a task has successive choices with (\(m\)) and (\(n\)) possibilities, there are (mn) combined outcomes. Factorial is (\(n!=n(n-1)...1\)), with (\(0!=1\)).

Order matters: permutations

The number of ordered selections of (\(r\)) distinct objects from (\(n\)) is (\(nP_r=n!/(n-r)!\)). For arranging all n distinct objects in a line, there are (n!) orders. With repeated identical objects, divide by each repeated-count factorial.

Order does not matter: combinations

The number of ways to choose r objects from n is (\(nC_r=n!/(r!(n-r)!)\)). Each chosen group is counted (r!) times by permutations, so divide by that overcount.

Worked example: Choose a president and secretary from 8 people: offices differ, so there are (\(8 \times 7=56\)) assignments. Choose a 2-person committee: order is irrelevant, so (\(8C_2=28\)).

sections.label: Methods and exam checks
sections.html:
• Ask whether swapping two selected people creates a new outcome.
  • Apply restrictions before counting; split into disjoint cases when needed.
  • For repeated letters, divide by factorials of identical-letter counts.
  • For a circle, rotations are considered the same in an ordinary round-table arrangement.
  • Check whether repetition is allowed in each position.

sections.label: Key facts and formulas
sections.html:
• (\(nP_r=n!/(n-r)!\)) and (\(nC_r=n!/(r!(n-r)!)\)).
  • (\(nC_r=nC_{n-r}\)); choosing a group equals choosing who is left out.
  • Number of circular arrangements of n distinct people is (\((n-1)!\)).
  • For identical objects, divide the total arrangements by the factorial for each repeated type.

sections.label: Worked practice
sections.html:
1. Core:

    How many ways can a team of 2 be chosen from 5 people?

    1. (\(5\))
    2. (\(10\))
    3. (\(20\))
    4. (\(25\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(10\))

    Order does not matter: (\(5C_2=5\cdot4/2=10\)).

  2. Core:

    How many ways can 3 distinct books be arranged from 5 distinct books?

    1. (\(10\))
    2. (\(20\))
    3. (\(60\))
    4. (\(125\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(60\))

    Order matters: (\(5P_3=5\cdot4\cdot3=60\)).

  3. Foundation:

    How many ways can 3 different books be arranged on a shelf?

    1. (\(3\))
    2. (\(6\))
    3. (\(9\))
    4. (\(27\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(6\))

    Order matters. There are (\(3!=3 \times 2 \times 1=6\)) arrangements.

  4. Standard:

    How many 2-person committees can be selected from 7 people?

    1. (\(14\))
    2. (\(21\))
    3. (\(42\))
    4. (\(49\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(21\))

    Order does not matter: (\(7C_2=7 \times 6/2=21\)).

  5. Challenge:

    How many distinct arrangements can be made from the letters of LEVEL?

    1. (\(20\))
    2. (\(30\))
    3. (\(60\))
    4. (\(120\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(30\))

    There are 5 letters with L repeated twice and E repeated twice. Count is (\(5!/(2!2!)=30\)).
